California voters will decide the state's next governor, choose candidates for several other statewide offices and weigh in on 14 propositions when they head to the polls on Tuesday.
The ballot includes proposals on wealth taxes, affordable housing, state budget reserves, election rules, homeownership, medical research and environmental regulations.
Here's what you need to know about the statewide races on the California ballot.
Governor
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is barred by term limits from seeking another term.
Becerra, a former California attorney general, served as U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration. He also represented a Los Angeles-area congressional district for 24 years. Becerra's most notable endorsements include Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Hilton is a former Fox News host who served as an adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron. Hilton has been formally endorsed in the race by President Trump.
Both candidates have centered their campaigns on affordability, though each has introduced vastly different proposals to address rising costs for residents.
Becerra and Hilton have differed in their approaches to lowering the state's gas prices, California's environmental policies, homelessness, healthcare and collaborating with the federal government on immigration.
Lieutenant governor
Democrat Fiona Ma and Republican Gloria Romero are running for lieutenant governor.
The lieutenant governor is first in the line of succession to the governor and serves in several state government roles, including as president of the state Senate, casting tie-breaking votes when necessary. The officeholder also serves on boards overseeing higher education.
Attorney general
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is facing Republican Michael Gates in Tuesday's election for the state's top law enforcement post.
Bonta, a Democrat, is seeking a second full term. Gates, a former Huntington Beach city attorney, has campaigned on public safety, including full enforcement of Proposition 36.
Bonta has been a leading figure in California's legal battles against the Trump administration (https://www.cbsnews.com/sacramento/news/california-rob-bonta-discusses-trump-first-100-days/) . His reelection campaign (https://robbonta.com/issues/) also emphasizes gun violence prevention, consumer protections and reproductive rights.
Gates served as Huntington Beach's elected city attorney for a decade and in 2025 worked in the Trump administration for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division. His campaign calls for (https://www.gates4ag.com/issues) stronger prosecution of repeat offenders, increased support for law enforcement and greater local control over housing decisions.
Secretary of State
Incumbent Democrat Shirley N. Weber and Republican Donald P. Wagner are competing in the race for secretary of state.
The secretary of state is California's chief elections officer, responsible for overseeing statewide elections, maintaining election-related records and administering campaign finance and lobbying disclosure requirements. The office also handles business filings and other official state records.
Weber's campaign has emphasized strengthening election security, protecting voting rights and maintaining access to voting. Wagner's campaign has also focused on election security, offering his support of Proposition 39, which aims to introduce new voter ID requirements. Weber has opposed that measure. Wagner has also pushed for faster results during the ballot counting process.
Insurance commissioner
Democrats Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor, and state Sen. Ben Allen are competing to become California's next insurance commissioner. The office is responsible for regulating the state's insurance industry, enforcing insurance laws and addressing consumer complaints.
The next commissioner will take office as California continues to grapple with rising insurance costs, wildfire-related losses and insurers limiting or withdrawing coverage in parts of the state.
The candidates have offered different approaches to addressing the insurance market, including questions about affordability, consumer protections and the availability of coverage.
Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara was unable to run for re-election due to term limits.
Superintendent of Public Instruction
Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are competing to become California's next superintendent of public instruction, succeeding Tony Thurmond, who reached his term limit.
The superintendent is the state's elected chief public school officer and leads the California Department of Education. The office oversees the implementation of state education policies and works with school districts and other education agencies.
Barrera is board president of the San Diego Unified School District, the nation's second-largest district, and has been endorsed by Thurmond. Shaw is a Chino Valley school board president who has been endorsed by Hilton and the Republican Party.
Shaw has vowed to cut bureaucratic waste, demand fiscal transparency and protect fairness in sports for girls. Her district was previously sued by California for adopting a gender notification policy.
Barrerra has touted his district's gains in graduation rates and various academic levels and said he looks forward to improving similar advancements across the state, if elected.
The position is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run under party labels on the ballot.
Board of Equalization
California voters will elect members of the State Board of Equalization, which oversees certain tax programs and provides property tax oversight and assistance to county assessors. It is the only board of its kind in the nation.
The board has four elected district members, and voters will choose a candidate for the district in which they live. The candidates on an individual ballot will depend on the voter's location.
Proposition 1: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for housing affordability programs
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to borrow $11.25 billion for housing programs, including affordable rental housing, supportive housing, homeownership and down-payment assistance, veterans' home loans, and housing for farmworkers, tribal communities and students.
The proposal includes funding to build and rehabilitate rental housing and preserve existing affordable units.
A yes vote would allow the state to issue the bonds. A no vote would prevent the borrowing.
The state is expected to pay between $500 million and $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the bonds.
Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.
The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period. A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns. No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.
Proposition 3: Makes a high-income tax increase permanent to fund schools and healthcare
Proposition 3 would make permanent an existing increase in state income tax rates for high-income earners. The tax applies to individuals earning more than a threshold initially set at $371,000 and adjusted annually for inflation.
The existing tax increase is set to expire in 2031. If approved, Proposition 3 would extend it indefinitely, maintaining an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue.
A yes vote would make the tax increase permanent. A no vote would allow it to expire in 2031 under current law.
Supporters including the California Teachers Association and California State PTA say the measure would protect funding for schools and healthcare. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, argue that making the tax permanent would increase the long-term tax burden and that the state should address spending concerns first.
Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money. Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs. A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.
Proposition 5: Changes the process for filling vacancies after statewide recall elections
Proposition 5 would change how California fills vacancies when voters recall a statewide elected official.
Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and select a replacement in the same election. The measure would separate those decisions, generally providing for a subsequent special election or an appointment.
A yes vote would remove the replacement candidate question from recall elections. A no vote would preserve the current process.
Supporters say the change would prevent a replacement from winning with only a small share of the vote and could reduce the political and administrative costs of recall elections. Opponents argue that it would take the decision away from voters at the time of a recall and could leave offices vacant while a replacement is selected.
Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price. Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds. A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments. The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.
Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research
Proposition 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund research into immunology and immunotherapy, including efforts to prevent and treat diseases.

Proposition 42 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution.
It began as Initiative #25-0039A1, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office.
Prop.
42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 (Billionaire Wealth Tax) on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.

Ban new taxes on personal property
Proposition 42 would make it much harder to create a wealth tax in California by prohibiting new taxes on the mere ownership of assets such as investment accounts, business interests and personal property — assets that are typically only taxed when they are sold or generate income. Like Proposition 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), which also attempts to block Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 42 would nullify Proposition 40 if it receives more votes, even if the billionaire tax also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Support
The measure’s ultra-wealthy backers say California should not tax people for merely owning or controlling retirement accounts, financial portfolios, or valuable personal possessions like art. They want to prevent taxes on unrealized gains — paper wealth that hasn’t been sold or generated taxable revenue — warning that pensions and retirement accounts could one day be taxed on their future value.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which is the sponsor of Prop. 40. The union argues that Prop. 42 is designed to trick voters into making it impossible to apply a wealth tax to billionaires. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on everyday people, the union says; instead, it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying a one-time tax on their huge wealth.

What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.
Broadly prohibiting retroactive taxation would hamstring the ability of state leaders to enact effective and timely tax policy changes that raise revenues needed to meet the needs of Californians.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 42?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 41 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/). The measure is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Professional Firefighters, and the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California.
There is no official opposition campaign for Prop. 41, but prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU-UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters are also opposed.

How Can Californians Make Sense of the Tax Measures on the November Ballot?
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Mary Severance (https://www.ppic.org/person/mary-severance/)
Five of the fourteen statewide initiatives on the November ballot are tax measures. What implications might these initiatives have, and how are voters feeling about them? These questions were the focus of a lunchtime discussion last week in Sacramento.
Mark Baldassare, director of the PPIC Statewide Survey, kicked off the event with key insights from the most recent survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/).
The bottom line on the tax measures? “California voters are giving the five tax measures mixed reviews. Four of the five have majority support—but they’re not big majorities; they’re not over 60%. So the outcome is very uncertain.”
Baldassare pointed to other survey findings that could factor into ballot choices. “Most Californians say that there are too many initiatives on the ballot, and that the ballot initiatives are confusing,” he said. “The default is to vote no if you’re unsure.”
More broadly still, Baldassare noted that Californians are feeling negative about where things are heading in the state and the nation: “Majorities expect bad economic times over the next 12 months, and there are low approval ratings for elected leaders and low trust in the federal and state governments.”
Baldassare’s briefing set the stage for a discussion between Tani Cantil-Sakauye, PPIC president and CEO; Gale Kaufman, president of Kaufman Strategies; and Rob Stutzman, founder and president of Stutzman Public Affairs.
Cantil-Sakauye asked the panelists about how the overall mood might affect election outcomes. “It’s as bad as I can remember in terms of the negativity,” said Kaufman. However, she added that if past experience holds, voters will do their research on each of the ballot measures. “They pick each one individually,” she said. “You can’t make a blanket statement.”
Stutzman noted that voter negativity extends to both parties. “As much as you’re hearing about the midterms dynamic being driven by how unpopular the president is,” he said, “you still have a very unpopular Democratic Party.”
The tax measure that has attracted the most voter interest so far is Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Stutzman noted that the strongest argument for Prop 40 is that too much wealth has been accumulated by too few people. But Kaufman said that the measure has been divisive: “The Yes side of 40 has fragmented the Democratic coalition of activists throughout the state.” As Stutzman pointed out, disagreement about the potential impact of Prop 40 “allows the No campaign to point out that Becerra, Hilton, and Newsom are all opposed . . . and say this must be a bad idea.”
While Proposition 3—which would extend a temporary marginal tax on high-income Californians—had majority support in PPIC’s September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), less than half of voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 43, which would raise the vote threshold for approving local taxes to two-thirds.
For Stutzman, the relative lack of support for Prop 43 was a bit unexpected: “I was a little surprised when I saw the numbers,” he said. “But I also know that the would-be Yes side is preparing to spend money to push this over the top.” Kaufman said she was not surprised. “Making it more difficult for local entities to be able to tax themselves,” she said, “has a huge impact on cities, counties and special districts, who are really in trouble.”
In the end, the panelists agreed that the sheer number of measures on the ballot could play a role in the outcome. “With 14 measures on the ballot,” said Kaufman, “I think there’s going to be tremendous confusion.”

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

California voters will decide the state's next governor, choose candidates for several other statewide offices and weigh in on 14 propositions when they head to the polls on Tuesday.
The ballot includes proposals on wealth taxes, affordable housing, state budget reserves, election rules, homeownership, medical research and environmental regulations.
Here's what you need to know about the statewide races on the California ballot.
Governor
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is barred by term limits from seeking another term.
Becerra, a former California attorney general, served as U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration. He also represented a Los Angeles-area congressional district for 24 years. Becerra's most notable endorsements include Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Hilton is a former Fox News host who served as an adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron. Hilton has been formally endorsed in the race by President Trump.
Both candidates have centered their campaigns on affordability, though each has introduced vastly different proposals to address rising costs for residents.
Becerra and Hilton have differed in their approaches to lowering the state's gas prices, California's environmental policies, homelessness, healthcare and collaborating with the federal government on immigration.
Lieutenant governor
Democrat Fiona Ma and Republican Gloria Romero are running for lieutenant governor.
The lieutenant governor is first in the line of succession to the governor and serves in several state government roles, including as president of the state Senate, casting tie-breaking votes when necessary. The officeholder also serves on boards overseeing higher education.
Attorney general
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is facing Republican Michael Gates in Tuesday's election for the state's top law enforcement post.
Bonta, a Democrat, is seeking a second full term. Gates, a former Huntington Beach city attorney, has campaigned on public safety, including full enforcement of Proposition 36.
Bonta has been a leading figure in California's legal battles against the Trump administration (https://www.cbsnews.com/sacramento/news/california-rob-bonta-discusses-trump-first-100-days/) . His reelection campaign (https://robbonta.com/issues/) also emphasizes gun violence prevention, consumer protections and reproductive rights.
Gates served as Huntington Beach's elected city attorney for a decade and in 2025 worked in the Trump administration for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division. His campaign calls for (https://www.gates4ag.com/issues) stronger prosecution of repeat offenders, increased support for law enforcement and greater local control over housing decisions.
Secretary of State
Incumbent Democrat Shirley N. Weber and Republican Donald P. Wagner are competing in the race for secretary of state.
The secretary of state is California's chief elections officer, responsible for overseeing statewide elections, maintaining election-related records and administering campaign finance and lobbying disclosure requirements. The office also handles business filings and other official state records.
Weber's campaign has emphasized strengthening election security, protecting voting rights and maintaining access to voting. Wagner's campaign has also focused on election security, offering his support of Proposition 39, which aims to introduce new voter ID requirements. Weber has opposed that measure. Wagner has also pushed for faster results during the ballot counting process.
Insurance commissioner
Democrats Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor, and state Sen. Ben Allen are competing to become California's next insurance commissioner. The office is responsible for regulating the state's insurance industry, enforcing insurance laws and addressing consumer complaints.
The next commissioner will take office as California continues to grapple with rising insurance costs, wildfire-related losses and insurers limiting or withdrawing coverage in parts of the state.
The candidates have offered different approaches to addressing the insurance market, including questions about affordability, consumer protections and the availability of coverage.
Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara was unable to run for re-election due to term limits.
Superintendent of Public Instruction
Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are competing to become California's next superintendent of public instruction, succeeding Tony Thurmond, who reached his term limit.
The superintendent is the state's elected chief public school officer and leads the California Department of Education. The office oversees the implementation of state education policies and works with school districts and other education agencies.
Barrera is board president of the San Diego Unified School District, the nation's second-largest district, and has been endorsed by Thurmond. Shaw is a Chino Valley school board president who has been endorsed by Hilton and the Republican Party.
Shaw has vowed to cut bureaucratic waste, demand fiscal transparency and protect fairness in sports for girls. Her district was previously sued by California for adopting a gender notification policy.
Barrerra has touted his district's gains in graduation rates and various academic levels and said he looks forward to improving similar advancements across the state, if elected.
The position is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run under party labels on the ballot.
Board of Equalization
California voters will elect members of the State Board of Equalization, which oversees certain tax programs and provides property tax oversight and assistance to county assessors. It is the only board of its kind in the nation.
The board has four elected district members, and voters will choose a candidate for the district in which they live. The candidates on an individual ballot will depend on the voter's location.
Proposition 1: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for housing affordability programs
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to borrow $11.25 billion for housing programs, including affordable rental housing, supportive housing, homeownership and down-payment assistance, veterans' home loans, and housing for farmworkers, tribal communities and students.
The proposal includes funding to build and rehabilitate rental housing and preserve existing affordable units.
A yes vote would allow the state to issue the bonds. A no vote would prevent the borrowing.
The state is expected to pay between $500 million and $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the bonds.
Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.
The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period. A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns. No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.
Proposition 3: Makes a high-income tax increase permanent to fund schools and healthcare
Proposition 3 would make permanent an existing increase in state income tax rates for high-income earners. The tax applies to individuals earning more than a threshold initially set at $371,000 and adjusted annually for inflation.
The existing tax increase is set to expire in 2031. If approved, Proposition 3 would extend it indefinitely, maintaining an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue.
A yes vote would make the tax increase permanent. A no vote would allow it to expire in 2031 under current law.
Supporters including the California Teachers Association and California State PTA say the measure would protect funding for schools and healthcare. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, argue that making the tax permanent would increase the long-term tax burden and that the state should address spending concerns first.
Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money. Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs. A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.
Proposition 5: Changes the process for filling vacancies after statewide recall elections
Proposition 5 would change how California fills vacancies when voters recall a statewide elected official.
Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and select a replacement in the same election. The measure would separate those decisions, generally providing for a subsequent special election or an appointment.
A yes vote would remove the replacement candidate question from recall elections. A no vote would preserve the current process.
Supporters say the change would prevent a replacement from winning with only a small share of the vote and could reduce the political and administrative costs of recall elections. Opponents argue that it would take the decision away from voters at the time of a recall and could leave offices vacant while a replacement is selected.
Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price. Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds. A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments. The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.
Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research
Proposition 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund research into immunology and immunotherapy, including efforts to prevent and treat diseases.

Proposition 42 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution.
It began as Initiative #25-0039A1, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office.
Prop.
42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 (Billionaire Wealth Tax) on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.

Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.

Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure.
